newsitem.title: FRANCE: Zaire's premier urges French support for elections.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's premier urges French support for elections.

text.p: Zaire's military premier bought a full page in the French daily Le Monde on Thursday to denounce alleged attempts to break up the country and urge every French citizen to back free elections in the face of a rebel onslaught.

As Laurent Kabila's rebels closed in on Kinshasa, General Likulia Bolongo accused him of relying on well-equipped foreign troops and mercenaries and said Zaire's neighbours were behind massacres of refugees.

Likulia, in an "Open Letter to French Citizens about Democracy in France and Zaire", accused unnamed "major political and economic powers" of trying to take over "our immense natural resources in order to exploit them for their own benefit."
He accused some of Zaire's "neighbours and others further away (of seeking) a true balkanisation of Zaire."
"The first results of this political will was unprecedented ethnic cleansing which has cost, according to the most reliable sources, 1.6 million lives since 1990," Likulia said.

The United Nations and aid workers have accused Kabila's Tutsi-led rebels of carrying out massacres among Hutu refugees who fled to Zaire from Rwanda in 1994 in fear of reprisals for the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

Without criticising President Mobutu Sese Seko by name, Likulia acknowledged discontent in Zaire "legitimately caused by an accumulation of wasted resources, management, political and social mistakes, and a too long transition towards democratisation".

Political disputes and poverty had hurt the morale of Zaire's armed forces, depriving them of the "jolt of national pride needed to make up for their shocking lack of resources and equipment in the face of foreign armies powerfully equipped, long trained and perfectly commanded, including by mercenary officers," he wrote.
The government says rebel forces who have seized most of Zaire are being held up by the army some 200 km (120 miles) east of Kinshasa.
But the rebels say they are much closer to the city, and said they will enter the capital and capture Mobutu if he has not left the country by Saturday.
Likulia, recalling that he had been fed Republican ideals during his studies in France, said: "Republican normality is, quite simply, the only path for Zaire.

He said he trusted every French person would feel solidarity with what he called "their 45 million cousins who make Zaire the world's second biggest French-speaking country" and to back Zaire's bid for democracy in free and fair elections.
